chapters.title: DBMS Introduction

topics.title: What is DBMS?
topics.learn: A Database Management System is software used to manage, store, retrieve, organize, and control data in databases.
topics.example: A college system can use a DBMS to store student details, attendance, marks, fees, and course information.
keyPoints: It provides controlled access to stored data.
It supports storing, retrieving, and updating data.
It helps applications interact with databases.

topics.title: Why Do We Need a DBMS?
topics.learn: A DBMS helps organize data and provides benefits such as security, reduced redundancy, transaction support, indexing, and scalability.
topics.example: Instead of keeping student information in many independent spreadsheets, a college can maintain related information in a centralized database.

topics.title: Security in DBMS
topics.learn: A DBMS can control what different users are allowed to see or modify.
topics.example: A fee clerk may see fee status while the principal may also be allowed to see marks.
keyPoints: Different users can have different permissions.
Access can be controlled at database level.

topics.title: Reducing Data Redundancy
topics.learn: A DBMS helps reduce unnecessary duplicate storage of the same information.
topics.example: Student details need not be repeatedly stored in separate files for every course or department.
keyPoints: Redundancy means unnecessary repetition of data.
Reducing redundancy can reduce inconsistent copies.
Database design techniques help control duplication.

topics.title: ACID Properties
topics.learn: ACID properties describe important guarantees provided by database transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.
topics.example: In a fee transfer, the debit and credit should be treated as one complete transaction rather than leaving only half of the operation completed.
keyPoints: Durability preserves committed changes after failures.

topics.title: Indexing
topics.learn: Indexes provide a faster way to locate rows instead of scanning the entire table.
topics.example: Searching for a student by Roll No can use an index rather than reading every student row.
keyPoints: Indexes store references used for faster searches.

topics.title: Scalability
topics.learn: Scalability refers to the ability of a database system to handle increasing amounts of data, users, and workload.
topics.example: A college portal may need to handle far more users during result publication than on an ordinary day.
keyPoints: Database systems may need to handle growing workloads.
Scaling can involve stronger machines or additional machines.
Scalability is important for growing applications.

topics.title: Popular Types of Databases
topics.learn: The notes describe relational, document, key-value, graph, time-series, and object-oriented databases.
topics.example: UPI transactions are described using relational databases, while temporary user sessions are given as an example for key-value storage.
keyPoints: Relational databases use tables and relationships.
Graph databases model nodes and connections.

selfCheck: Why is security important in a DBMS?
What problem does data redundancy create?
Explain ACID in your own words.
Give one example of a key-value database use case.

chapters.title: DBMS Architecture

topics.title: What is DBMS Architecture?
topics.learn: DBMS architecture describes where software components reside and how they communicate.
topics.example: A database application may contain a client, an application server, and a database server.

topics.title: One-Tier Architecture
topics.learn: In one-tier architecture, the user interface and database engine run on the same machine.
topics.example: A Python application using SQLite on one computer.
keyPoints: It is suitable for a single-user environment.
Local resources are consumed by the application and database.

topics.title: Two-Tier Architecture
topics.learn: In two-tier architecture, a client application communicates directly with a database server.
topics.example: A Java desktop application connecting directly to MySQL.
keyPoints: Client directly communicates with database server.
ODBC or JDBC may manage connections.
The database is directly exposed to clients.

topics.title: Three-Tier Architecture
topics.learn: In three-tier architecture, the client communicates with an application server, which communicates with the database server.
topics.example: A mobile application calls a Node.js REST API, which then queries PostgreSQL.
keyPoints: Client does not directly access the database.
Application server sits in the middle.

topics.title: Distributed Databases
topics.learn: A distributed database stores data segments on geographically separated servers while presenting them as one logical database.
topics.example: Different university campuses maintain local attendance data on local servers.
keyPoints: Data can exist on multiple servers.
The system can appear as one logical database.
Synchronization can be asynchronous or transaction-based.

topics.title: CAP Theorem
topics.learn: The notes describe Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance and explain a trade-off between Consistency and Availability in distributed systems.
topics.example: The notes discuss UPI-style payments and digital notice boards as different distributed-system scenarios.
keyPoints: Consistency means nodes reflect identical data at a given moment.
Availability means requests receive timely responses.
Partition Tolerance means operation continues despite communication disruption.
The notes treat Partition Tolerance as mandatory in distributed systems.
The discussed trade-off is between Consistency and Availability.

selfCheck: Differentiate one-tier, two-tier, and three-tier architecture.
Why is an application server useful in three-tier architecture?
Explain Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.

chapters.title: Data Abstraction

topics.title: What is Data Abstraction?
topics.learn: Data abstraction hides implementation details from users and applications while exposing relevant data structures and operations.
topics.example: A student can view attendance without knowing how the records are stored on disk.

topics.title: Physical Level
topics.learn: The physical level describes how data is actually stored, including file structures, indexing, blocks, and storage details.
topics.example: Attendance records may be stored in blocks on SSD storage with indexes.
keyPoints: Includes file structures and data blocks.
Users normally do not see it.

topics.title: Logical Level
topics.learn: The logical level describes tables, columns, data types, relationships, and constraints.
topics.example: A Students table contains Roll No, Name, and relationships to Courses.
keyPoints: Developers commonly work with this level.

topics.title: View Level
topics.learn: The view level presents customized subsets of data to different users.
topics.example: A warden sees Roll No, Name, and Fee Status while the examination branch sees marks.
keyPoints: Different users may see different information.

topics.title: Logical Data Independence
topics.learn: Logical data independence allows logical schema changes without requiring application programs to be rewritten.
topics.example: An Address field is split into Street, City, and Pin Code without rewriting dependent applications.
keyPoints: Applications are insulated from some schema changes.

topics.title: Physical Data Independence
topics.learn: Physical data independence allows physical storage changes without affecting the logical schema.
topics.example: Attendance data is moved from HDD to SSD and a new index is added without changing SQL queries.

topics.title: Physical → Logical → View
topics.learn: The hierarchy moves from physical storage to logical structure to user-specific views.
topics.example: A mobile portal shows a view while developers manage the logical structure and the database server manages physical storage.
keyPoints: Higher levels should be insulated from lower-level changes.

selfCheck: Differentiate physical, logical, and view levels.

chapters.title: Types of Data Models

topics.title: What is a Data Model?
topics.learn: A data model provides a formal way to describe how facts are organized inside a database.
topics.example: Choosing a relational model gives a table-based structure, while a graph model represents nodes and edges.
keyPoints: A model describes organization of data.
The choice influences flexibility and maintenance.

topics.title: Hierarchical Model
topics.learn: A hierarchical model organizes records in a strict parent-child tree.
topics.example: University → College → Department → Course → Student.

topics.title: Network Model
topics.learn: A network model allows records to have multiple parents and supports complex many-to-many associations.
topics.example: Students belong to several clubs and clubs have many students.

topics.title: Relational Model
topics.learn: The relational model stores data in tables made of rows and columns and uses keys to represent relationships.
topics.example: STUDENT, COURSE, and MARKS tables linked using keys.
keyPoints: SQL is used with relational databases.

topics.title: Object-Oriented Model
topics.learn: The object-oriented model persists programming objects together with their attributes and behavior.
topics.example: A robotics system can store Robot objects containing Sensor objects.
keyPoints: Keeps object structures close to application objects.

topics.title: Entity–Relationship Model
topics.learn: The ER model is a diagrammatic blueprint for representing entities, attributes, and relationships during conceptual design.
topics.example: Student and Course connected through ENROLLED_IN.

selfCheck: What makes a relational model table-oriented?
Where is an ER model useful?

chapters.title: ER Model

topics.title: Purpose of ER Model
topics.learn: The ER model provides a conceptual-level blueprint of entities, attributes, and relationships before physical implementation.
topics.example: Designing Student, Course, Instructor, and their relationships before creating SQL tables.
keyPoints: Bridges real-world requirements and database design.

topics.title: Entities and Entity Sets
topics.learn: An entity represents a real-world object. An entity set is a collection of similar entities.
topics.example: One Student is an entity; all students together form the Student entity set.
keyPoints: Strong entities have their own identifying key.
Weak entities depend on another entity.

topics.title: Attributes
topics.learn: Attributes describe properties of entities.
topics.example: Student can have Roll No, Name, Programme, and phone numbers.
keyPoints: A key attribute identifies an entity.
Multivalued attributes can contain multiple values.

topics.title: Relationships and Relationship Sets
topics.learn: A relationship represents a logical association among entities, while a relationship set contains instances of such associations.
topics.example: Student ENROLLED_IN Course.
keyPoints: Binary relationships involve two entity types.

topics.title: ER Diagram Notation
topics.learn: ER diagrams use shapes to represent entities, attributes, and relationships.
topics.example: Rectangles represent entity sets, ellipses represent attributes, and diamonds represent relationships.

topics.title: Weak Entities, Cardinality and Participation
topics.learn: Weak entities depend on identifying relationships. Relationships can have different cardinalities such as one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many.
topics.example: A weak occupancy record may depend on a hostel room for identification.
keyPoints: Weak entities depend on strong entities.
Cardinality describes how many entities can participate.
1:1, 1:N, and M:N are common relationship forms.
Participation describes involvement in a relationship.

topics.title: Aggregation
topics.learn: Aggregation treats a relationship set and its participating entities as a higher-level unit that can participate in another relationship.
topics.example: A relationship between Student and Course can be treated as a higher-level unit for another relationship.
keyPoints: Combines a relationship and its participating entities conceptually.

selfCheck: What is the purpose of an ER model?

chapters.title: Relational Model

topics.title: Domain, Attribute, Tuple and Relation
topics.learn: The relational model is built from domains, attributes, tuples, and relations.
topics.example: A STUDENT table contains attributes such as RollNo and Name and rows representing students.
keyPoints: Domain is a set of valid values.

topics.title: Schema vs Instance
topics.learn: A schema describes the permanent structure of a relation while an instance represents the current rows in the table.
topics.example: The STUDENT schema defines columns and constraints; today's student rows form its current instance.
keyPoints: Instances change as rows are inserted or deleted.

topics.title: Integrity Constraints
topics.learn: Relational databases use constraints to protect valid data and relationships.
topics.example: A primary key cannot be NULL, and a foreign key should match an existing referenced key.
keyPoints: Entity integrity prevents NULL primary keys.

topics.title: Designing a STUDENT Relation
topics.learn: A relational table can model student information using attributes, primary keys, and domains.
topics.example: STUDENT(RollNo, Name, Programme, MobileNo).
keyPoints: Each column has a defined domain.

selfCheck: Define domain, attribute, tuple, and relation.

chapters.title: Types of Keys

topics.title: Super Key
topics.learn: A super key is a column set that uniquely identifies rows and may contain redundant columns.
topics.example: RollNo, or a set such as RollNo + MobileNo.

topics.title: Candidate Key
topics.learn: A candidate key is a minimal super key; removing an attribute destroys uniqueness.
topics.example: RollNo or Email can each be candidate keys if each uniquely identifies a student.
keyPoints: Every candidate key is a super key.

topics.title: Primary Key
topics.learn: The primary key is the candidate key selected as the official row identifier.
topics.example: A college may choose RollNo as the primary key of STUDENT.

topics.title: Alternate Key
topics.learn: An alternate key is a candidate key that was not selected as the primary key.
topics.example: If RollNo is primary and Email is also a candidate key, Email is an alternate key.
keyPoints: It is still a candidate key.
It was simply not selected as primary.

topics.title: Composite Key
topics.learn: A composite key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row.
topics.example: MARKS can use RollNo + CourseCode as a composite key.
keyPoints: Individual columns may not be unique.

topics.title: Foreign Key
topics.learn: A foreign key references a key in another table and helps establish relationships between tables.
topics.example: MARKS.RollNo references STUDENT.RollNo.
keyPoints: Can be NULL when the relationship is optional according to the notes.

selfCheck: Why must a candidate key be minimal?
Why is a foreign key needed?

topics.title: Why Normalisation?
topics.learn: Normalisation organizes relations to reduce redundancy and dependency problems while preserving useful relationships.
topics.example: A large marks table containing repeated student and course details can be split into STUDENT, COURSE, and RESULT tables.
keyPoints: Uses functional dependencies to guide decomposition.

topics.title: Functional Dependencies
topics.learn: A functional dependency describes how one attribute set determines another.
topics.example: RollNo → StudentName, Programme.
keyPoints: Functional dependencies help identify normalization problems.
The notes use several dependencies in the student-course example.

topics.title: First Normal Form (1NF)
topics.learn: 1NF requires every cell to hold one value and repeating lists to be separated into individual rows.
topics.example: Instead of storing multiple course codes in one student cell, each course appears as a separate row.

topics.title: Second Normal Form (2NF)
topics.learn: 2NF removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key.
topics.example: In a result table with RollNo + CourseCode as a composite key, student details should not remain as partial dependencies.
keyPoints: Student and Course information can be separated.

topics.title: Third Normal Form (3NF)
topics.learn: 3NF removes transitive dependencies.
topics.example: If CourseCode determines InstructorID and InstructorID determines InstructorName, InstructorName should be separated into an INSTRUCTOR table.
keyPoints: Non-key attributes should not depend transitively on the key.

topics.title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
topics.learn: In BCNF, for every functional dependency X → Y, X must be a candidate key.
topics.example: The notes use an instructor-course relationship to show when a BCNF violation may occur.
keyPoints: Every determinant must be a candidate key.
Decomposition may be required to resolve violations.

topics.title: Lossless Join and Dependency Preservation
topics.learn: A decomposition should ideally allow reconstruction of the original relation without losing information while preserving important dependencies.
topics.example: The normalized STUDENT, COURSE, INSTRUCTOR, and RESULT relations can be joined without losing the original facts according to the notes.
keyPoints: Dependency preservation keeps important dependencies enforceable.
Both are important considerations in decomposition.

chapters.title: Denormalization

topics.title: What is Denormalization?
topics.learn: Denormalization intentionally introduces controlled redundancy to make common queries faster or simpler.
topics.example: A RESULT_FLAT table can contain student, course, instructor, and grade information together for frequently used reports.
keyPoints: The normalized source of truth should remain known.

topics.title: When and Why to Denormalize
topics.learn: The notes describe denormalization as useful for heavy-read, light-write workloads, repeated aggregates, and reporting.
topics.example: A placement dashboard frequently reads CGPA information but updates it only occasionally.
keyPoints: Useful for heavy reads and lighter writes.

topics.title: Performance vs Redundancy
topics.learn: Denormalization can improve read speed but usually increases storage and update complexity.
topics.example: A flat report table may make reads faster but requires synchronization when source data changes.

topics.title: RESULT_FLAT Example
topics.learn: The notes show a denormalized result report combining fields from multiple normalized tables.
topics.example: RESULT_FLAT can contain RollNo, StudentName, Programme, CourseCode, CourseName, Credits, InstructorName, and Grade.

topics.title: Safe Denormalization Guidelines
topics.learn: The notes recommend measuring actual query performance, targeting hot paths, automating refreshes, documenting duplicated data, and maintaining a rollback plan.
topics.example: Use EXPLAIN and actual timings before choosing to duplicate data.

selfCheck: Why can duplicated data become stale?
Why should performance be measured before denormalizing?

chapters.title: Transactions & Concurrency Control

topics.title: What is a Transaction?
topics.learn: A transaction is a small complete job that the database treats as one package.
topics.example: Publishing a result may require inserting grades, recalculating CGPA, and setting a published flag.
keyPoints: Partial completion should not leave inconsistent state.

topics.title: ACID Properties
topics.learn: Transactions use Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability guarantees.
topics.example: A fee payment should either complete properly or be rolled back.
keyPoints: Isolation = transactions do not improperly interfere.

topics.title: Transaction Life Cycle
topics.learn: Transactions pass through states such as ACTIVE, PARTIALLY COMMITTED, COMMITTED, and ABORTED.
topics.example: A transaction becomes committed after successful completion or aborted after failure.
keyPoints: PARTIALLY COMMITTED means the final statement finished.

topics.title: Serial and Interleaved Schedules
topics.learn: Transactions may execute serially or with interleaved operations.
topics.example: T1 then T2 is serial; T1 step, T2 step, T1 step is interleaved.

topics.title: Serializability
topics.learn: A schedule is serializable when its result is equivalent to some serial execution.
topics.example: Conflict-serializability can be analyzed using a precedence graph.
keyPoints: Conflict-serializable schedules can be tested using a graph.
A cycle in the conflict graph indicates a problem for conflict serializability.

topics.title: Isolation Problems
topics.learn: Concurrent transactions can create anomalies such as dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads.
topics.example: A transaction reads a fee change that another transaction later rolls back.
keyPoints: Non-repeatable read gets different values for the same row.
Phantom read occurs when a repeated query returns a different set of rows.

topics.title: Isolation Levels
topics.learn: The notes describe Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable levels.
topics.example: Read Committed blocks dirty reads while Serializable provides stronger protection against anomalies.
keyPoints: Serializable provides the strongest level described in the notes.

topics.title: Concurrency Control Techniques
topics.learn: The notes cover shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking, timestamp ordering, and optimistic control.
topics.example: A teacher can hold an exclusive lock while changing a grade and another transaction must wait.
keyPoints: Optimistic control checks conflicts at commit.

topics.title: Database Recovery
topics.learn: Recovery techniques restore databases after transaction, system, media, or larger failures.
topics.example: A fee portal can use logs to recover after a crash.
keyPoints: Backup and restore are basic recovery techniques.
Shadow paging keeps an older consistent version.

selfCheck: Explain dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads.

chapters.title: SQL Commands

topics.title: SQL Command Families
topics.learn: The notes divide SQL commands into DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL families.
topics.example: DDL defines structure, DML manipulates rows, DCL manages access, and TCL manages transaction boundaries.

topics.title: DDL Commands
topics.learn: DDL defines or modifies database structure.
topics.example: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN phoneNo CHAR(10).
keyPoints: TRUNCATE removes table contents according to its command semantics.

topics.title: DML Commands
topics.learn: DML manipulates database rows.
topics.example: INSERT adds a student, UPDATE changes a grade, DELETE removes a row, and SELECT retrieves data.

topics.title: DCL Commands
topics.learn: DCL manages permissions and access control.
topics.example: GRANT or REVOKE privileges for database users.

topics.title: TCL Commands
topics.learn: TCL manages transaction boundaries and transaction control.
topics.example: SAVEPOINT can create a point to which a transaction can roll back.
keyPoints: SET TRANSACTION can configure transaction behavior.

topics.title: SQL Operators
topics.learn: SQL operators compare, combine, and calculate values while queries execute.
topics.example: WHERE pay BETWEEN 100000 AND 500000.
keyPoints: IN, BETWEEN, and LIKE are useful filtering operators.

topics.title: Aggregate Functions
topics.learn: Aggregate functions process sets of rows and return summarized values.
topics.example: COUNT(*) counts rows and SUM(pay) calculates total payroll.

topics.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
topics.learn: GROUP BY creates groups for aggregate calculations and HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
topics.example: GROUP BY division and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 can identify repeated role or division conditions.

selfCheck: Differentiate DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL.
Write examples of INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.
What is the purpose of GROUP BY?
Why is HAVING different from WHERE?

chapters.title: Indexing, SQL Optimisation, Sharding

topics.title: Why Optimise SQL Queries?
topics.learn: Slow queries can increase page load time, server load, and cloud costs. Query optimization aims to reduce unnecessary work.
topics.example: A merit-list page should retrieve only the columns it needs instead of SELECT *.

topics.title: Select Only Needed Columns
topics.learn: Avoid retrieving columns that are not required by the application.
topics.example: A merit page may need RollNo, Name, and CGPA rather than every student column.

topics.title: Filter Early, Join Later
topics.learn: Applying filters before large joins can reduce the amount of data processed.
topics.example: Filter students to the CSE 2023 batch before joining with placement information.

topics.title: Index Types
topics.learn: The notes distinguish primary or clustered indexes from secondary or non-clustered indexes.
topics.example: A primary index can be associated with RollNo while a secondary index can help find students by mobile number.
keyPoints: Primary/clustered indexing is associated with physical ordering.

topics.title: B-Tree and B+-Tree
topics.learn: B-tree structures guide searches through internal nodes while B+-tree leaves are linked to support efficient range scans.
topics.example: CGPA BETWEEN 8 AND 9 can be served efficiently using linked B+-tree leaves.
keyPoints: B-tree uses internal nodes to guide searches.
B+-tree leaves are linked for range scans.

topics.title: Vertical Scaling
topics.learn: Vertical scaling improves a single machine by adding resources such as RAM, CPU, or faster storage.
topics.example: Adding RAM and SSD capacity to a database server.
keyPoints: Resources may include CPU, RAM, and storage.

topics.title: Horizontal Scaling
topics.learn: Horizontal scaling adds more machines and can distribute or copy data across them.
topics.example: Adding additional servers to handle increased user traffic.

topics.title: Sharding
topics.learn: Sharding divides a large database into smaller independent pieces called shards.
topics.example: Delhi campus records are stored on one server and Mumbai campus records on another.
keyPoints: Each shard holds part of the data.

topics.title: Sharding Methods
topics.learn: The notes describe range-based, hashed, and directory sharding.
topics.example: Roll numbers can be divided into ranges, admission IDs can be hashed, or a directory can map course IDs to servers.
keyPoints: Range-based sharding divides by value ranges.
Hash-based sharding aims for even distribution.
Directory sharding uses a mapping table.

topics.title: RBAC, Encryption and Data Masking
topics.learn: The notes cover role-based access control, encryption, and multiple masking techniques for protecting sensitive data.
topics.example: Students, faculty, and admins receive different roles; sensitive account information can be encrypted or masked in test environments.
keyPoints: Encryption can protect data at rest, in transit, or at column level.
Masking can protect sensitive values in non-production data.
Masking types include dynamic, deterministic, non-deterministic, format-preserving, shuffling, redaction, and nulling.

selfCheck: Why should SQL queries be optimized?

chapters.title: SQL Queries Practice

topics.title: SELECT, Aliases and DISTINCT
topics.learn: Practice retrieving columns, renaming result columns, and returning unique values.
topics.example: SELECT given_name AS EMPLOYEE_NAME FROM staff; and SELECT DISTINCT division FROM staff;

topics.title: String Functions
topics.learn: Practice string transformation and extraction functions.
topics.example: UPPER, SUBSTRING, INSTR, RTRIM, LTRIM, REPLACE, CONCAT, and LENGTH.
keyPoints: SUBSTRING extracts part of a string.

topics.title: WHERE, IN, LIKE and BETWEEN
topics.learn: Use filtering operators to find specific rows.
topics.example: WHERE given_name IN ('Arjun', 'Rohan') or pay BETWEEN 100000 AND 500000.
keyPoints: IN matches a list of values.

topics.title: ORDER BY and LIMIT
topics.learn: Sort query results and restrict the number of returned rows.
topics.example: ORDER BY pay DESC LIMIT 5 returns the top five highest-paid employees.

topics.title: Date and Numeric Queries
topics.learn: Practice filtering by dates, salary ranges, and numeric properties.
topics.example: Find workers who joined in February 2014 using YEAR and MONTH.
keyPoints: MOD can identify odd or even IDs.

topics.title: GROUP BY and Aggregation Practice
topics.learn: Use COUNT, SUM, and other aggregates with GROUP BY.
topics.example: Show each division with its employee count ordered from highest to lowest.
keyPoints: ORDER BY can sort aggregate results.

topics.title: JOIN Queries
topics.learn: Practice combining rows from multiple tables.
topics.example: Join staff and role on staff_id to find employees who are Supervisors.
keyPoints: LEFT JOIN can reveal rows missing from another table.

topics.title: Subqueries and Top-N Problems
topics.learn: Practice nested queries, maximum salary queries, nth-highest salary, and grouped totals.
topics.example: Find employees earning the maximum salary using MAX, or compute an nth-highest salary using the provided pattern.
keyPoints: Subqueries can be nested inside SELECT, WHERE, or other query positions.
MAX can find the highest salary.
LIMIT/OFFSET can implement simple top-N retrieval.
The notes also provide a generic nth-highest salary formula.

selfCheck: Use LIKE to find names containing a letter.
Find the top five highest-paid employees.
